title: Hidden Edge 4
content:
"A coffin's for dead people, obviously," Wei Wuxian said. "My guess? The body buried here originally belonged to Jin Guangyao's mother, Meng Shi. He showed up tonight to dig her up so they could sail for the Eastern Seas together."

Lan Xichen went utterly still, staring blankly.

Nie Huaisang let out a quiet "Ah," nodding as if a light had just flickered on in his head. "Right. Yeah, that actually makes a lot of sense."

Wei Wuxian tilted his head. "So what do you think happened to her body after whoever took it dug it up? What would they do with it?"

"Why do you keep asking me, Wei-xiong?" Nie Huaisang whined, throwing his hands out. "You can interrogate me all day, but if I don't know, I don't know!"

He paused, biting his lip. "Then again..."

Taking his time, Nie Huaisang casually smoothed back a few stray locks of rain-soaked hair. "I mean, if this person hated Jin Guangyao that much, they'd probably be ruthless with the one thing he cared about most, right? Extra vicious, I'd bet."

"Like ripping her limb from limb and scattering the pieces across the countryside? Just like what happened to Chifeng-zun?"

Nie Huaisang’s eyes blew wide. He scrambled back a few steps, stammering, "T-t-that... that's way too sick..."

Wei Wuxian pinned him with an unreadable gaze for a long second before quietly looking away.

A hunch was just a hunch. Nobody had a scrap of proof.

Maybe Nie Huaisang's helpless, bewildered act really was just a mask. Maybe he refused to own up to treating living people like pawns on a board, or maybe his endgame reached far beyond this temple—hiding his real claws so he could climb to even greater heights. Or maybe things weren't that twisted at all. Maybe the blackmailer, the phantom hunter who butchered the cats, and the person who stitched Nie Mingjue back together were entirely someone else, and Nie Huaisang truly was just the spineless, useless coward he seemed to be.

For all they knew, Jin Guangyao's parting accusations were nothing more than a desperate, venomous bluff—scrambling to spin a lie the second Nie Huaisang blew his cover, deliberately unhinging Lan Xichen's mind so he could drag him into the pit to burn together. Jin Guangyao was a habitual liar with a ledger drenched in filth; him spinning a yarn at any given moment surprised absolutely no one.

And as for why he had changed his mind at the final second and shoved Lan Xichen out of harm's way? Who could ever crawl inside his head to find out?

Lan Xichen pressed the back of his hand hard against his temple, the veins bulging across his skin. His voice came out muffled, cracking under the weight of sheer exhaustion. "...What did he actually want? I used to think I understood him. Then I realized I didn't know him at all. Before tonight, I thought I finally had him figured out again, but now... I'm completely lost."

Nobody answered.

"What was he after?" Lan Xichen whispered to the empty air, hollowed out.

If the person closest to him in this world didn't have a clue, how could anyone else pretend to have the answers?

After a thick, suffocating quiet, Wei Wuxian broke the silence. "Well, standing around staring at each other isn't fixing anything. A few of us should head out to fetch backup, and the rest stay put to keep an eye on this mess. A wooden box and a handful of guqin strings aren't going to hold Chifeng-zun for long."

Right on cue, a violent shudder racked the heavy coffin. A series of muffled, concussive thuds hammered against the underside, vibrating with raw, unbridled fury.

Nie Huaisang flinched, shrinking into himself.

Wei Wuxian shot him a dry look. "See? We need to haul in a reinforced casket, dig a deeper pit, and bury him under real wards. At least a hundred years before anyone even thinks about cracking it open. If that thing ever sees the light of day, all hell will break loose..."

Before he could finish the sentence, a booming, brassy bark echoed from the street outside.

Wei Wuxian’s face drained of color in a heartbeat.

Jin Ling, on the other hand, instantly perked up, a spark returning to his eyes. "Fairy!"

The thunder had rolled away, and the torrential downpour had tapered off into a quiet, misty drizzle. The blackest hours of the night were behind them, a pale, milky dawn beginning to bleed over the horizon.

A wet, black-maned spiritual hound tore through the shattered doorway like a streak of dark wind, launching itself straight at Jin Ling. Its glossy eyes were round and dewy. Rearing up on its hind legs, it planted its front paws firmly against Jin Ling’s thighs, letting out a barrage of needy, whimpering yips.

Wei Wuxian caught sight of that slick, bright-red tongue lolling past rows of gleaming, razor-sharp fangs, relentlessly licking at Jin Ling’s hands. His vision went completely flat, lips parting as if his soul were about to billow straight out of his mouth in a wisp of blue smoke.

Without a word, Lan Wangji stepped smoothly into his line of sight, planting his broad frame between Wei Wuxian and the hound.

Moments later, the heavy clatter of boots announced a swarm of hundreds of cultivators locking down the perimeter of the Guanyin Temple. Every single one had their blade drawn, faces taut with hair-trigger focus, ready to breach and slaughter. But when the vanguard barged through the doors, the scene inside brought everyone to a dead halt.

The ones lying down were stone-cold dead; the ones left breathing were half-collapsed or barely leaning against pillars. In short: corpses everywhere, and an absolute disaster of a crime scene.

Leading the charge with bare steel were two familiar figures. On the left stood a senior manager of the Yunmeng Jiang Sect; on the right was none other than Lan Qiren himself.

Lan Qiren’s face was a storm of suspicion and bewilderment, but before he could bark out an order, his eyes locked onto Lan Wangji—who was practically glued flush against Wei Wuxian.

In a fraction of a second, every question in Lan Qiren's head vanished into thin air. A furious flush rushed straight to his cheeks, his brows angling into a furious V as he huffed and sputtered, his white goatee trembling violently as it floated on his furious huffs.

The Jiang steward scrambled over to Jiang Cheng, fussing in a panic, "Sect Leader! Are you alright..."

Lan Qiren, meanwhile, brandished his sword, voice booming: "Wei—"

Before the name could clear his lungs, a blur of pristine white robes shot past him from behind.

"Hanguang-jun!"

"Senior Wei!"

"Grandmaster Wei!"

A trailing disciple clipped Lan Qiren’s shoulder on his way through, nearly sending the old man tumbling sideways. Steam practically poured from Lan Qiren’s ears: "No running! No clamoring in the halls!"

Aside from Lan Wangji offering a quiet, dutiful "Uncle," not a single soul paid him the slightest bit of attention.

Lan Sizhui had a death-grip on Lan Wangji’s left sleeve with one hand and Wei Wuxian’s forearm with the other, beaming ear to ear. "Thank goodness! Hanguang-jun, Senior Wei, you're both unhurt! Fairy was in such a complete panic, we were terrified you'd walked into a catastrophic trap!"

Lan Jingyi rolled his eyes. "Sizhui, are you out of your mind? As if there's a single problem in this world Hanguang-jun can't handle! Told you that you were fretting over nothing."

"Jingyi, pretty sure you were the one having a nervous breakdown the entire flight over."

"Shut up! Stop talking nonsense!"

Catching sight of Wen Ning finally dragging himself up from the floor out of the corner of his eye, Lan Sizhui immediately reached out, pulling him straight into the flock of juniors, everyone chattering over one another to piece the story together.

Turns out, after Fairy had bitten Su She, the hound had bolted through the streets until it tracked down a minor subsidiary clan under Yunmeng Jiang stationed near town, barking like mad outside their gates. The young sect leader saw the custom collar, the gold badge, and the clan crest, instantly recognizing the beast as highborn property. Seeing the blood caked across its fangs and coat from a brutal scrap, he knew whoever owned the dog was likely in mortal danger. Not daring to drag his feet, he hopped on his sword and flew straight to Lotus Pier to alert the true powerhouse of the region: the Yunmeng Jiang Sect. The senior steward took one look and recognized Jin Ling's prized spiritual hound, immediately mobilizing a rescue squad.

Around the same time, the Gusu Lan contingent was just about to depart Lotus Pier when Fairy cut off their path. Rearing up, the dog tore a narrow strip of white fabric from the hem of Lan Sizhui’s robes, nudging it onto its own forehead with a paw—trying to twist the scrap into a makeshift circle around its brow—before flopping onto the dirt to play dead. Lan Qiren had been completely baffled, but Lan Sizhui had connected the dots in a flash: Teacher, look at it! Doesn't that look like it's mimicking our forehead ribbon? Is it trying to tell us Hanguang-jun or our disciples are in trouble?

And so, Yunmeng Jiang, Gusu Lan, and several other clans who hadn't packed up yet pooled their disciples and rushed to the scene together.

Lan Jingyi clicked his tongue in genuine awe. "We always thought 'Fairy' was a gimmick, but damn, that really is a magical beast!"

Magical beast or not, Wei Wuxian thought, shivering behind Lan Wangji’s back, it’s still a dog, which means it’s the most terrifying demon on this planet.

Ever since the Lan juniors had crowded into the hall, Jin Ling had been sneaking glances their way, watching them cluster around Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji in a noisy, lively circle. Noticing how pale Wei Wuxian was looking, Jin Ling gave Fairy’s flank a quiet pat, muttering under his breath, "Fairy. Outside."

Fairy wagged its tail, trying to sneak another lick across his knuckles. Jin Ling gave it a stern look. "Go on! Out! You ignoring me now?"

The hound shot him a tragic, wounded look, but turned around and trotted out through the shattered doors, tail tucked.

Wei Wuxian finally let out the breath he’d been holding.

Jin Ling shifted on his feet, wanting to walk over, but too embarrassed to make the move. While he was hesitating, Lan Sizhui’s gaze drifted down to Wei Wuxian’s waist. He froze, blinking in disbelief. "...Senior Wei?"

Wei Wuxian perked up. "Hm? What is it?"

Lan Sizhui stared, dazed. "That... that flute. May I take a closer look?"

Wei Wuxian unhooked it, curious. "What's wrong with it?"

Lan Sizhui took the flute with both hands, his brow knitting together in quiet, conflicted confusion. Lan Wangji watched him steadily. Wei Wuxian glanced at Lan Wangji, amused. "What's gotten into your boy? He have an eye for instruments?"

Lan Jingyi gasped, eyes widening. "Wait! You finally ditched that tone-deaf, ugly piece of junk? Wow, this new one looks incredible!"

The poor kid had no idea that this "incredible new flute" was the very legendary, terrifying artifact he’d spent half his life dreaming of laying eyes on: the Ghost Flute, Chenqing. He was just secretly celebrating: Thank heavens! At least he won't embarrass Hanguang-jun when they play duets together now. God, that old bamboo stick was hideous, and the pitch was atrocious!

Lan Wangji murmured softly, "Sizhui."

Lan Sizhui snapped out of his trance. Offering Chenqing back with both hands, he bowed. "Senior Wei."

Wei Wuxian took the instrument, suddenly remembering who had handed it back to him. Turning toward Jiang Cheng, he offered a casual, "Thanks." He gave Chenqing a little flourish. "This... mind if I keep it?"

Jiang Cheng looked at him, his face hard. "It was yours to begin with."

He lingered, his lips twitching slightly as though he had something more to spit out, but Wei Wuxian was already turning back to Lan Wangji. Seeing that, Jiang Cheng swallowed his words, sinking into silence.

Around the hall, people were busy: some securing the perimeter, some adding fresh binding arrays to the heavy coffin, some figuring out how to safely transport the cursed box, and others just aggressively nursing their fury.

Lan Qiren barked, "Xichen! What on earth happened to you?!"

Lan Xichen pressed a thumb against his temple, his brows tangled in unspeakable sorrow. "Uncle... please," he rasped, utterly spent. "Don't ask. Truly. I really don't have the strength to say a single word right now."

Lan Qiren had raised Lan Xichen with his own two hands, and he had never once seen the boy this frayed, this utterly stripped of grace. Looking at his older nephew, then glancing over at Lan Wangji surrounded by kids with Wei Wuxian glued to his hip, the old teacher felt a cold, furious fire roaring in his chest. Both of his crowning achievements—the peerless Twin Jades of Gusu—had completely slipped out of his grasp, each finding their own way to drive him into an early grave.

The coffin entombing Nie Mingjue and Jin Guangyao was ridiculously heavy, not to mention a volatile hazard that required kid gloves, so a few visiting sect leaders took it upon themselves to oversee the heavy lifting.

One sect leader caught a glimpse of the Guanyin statue strapped on top, blinking in surprise before pointing it out like a carnival attraction: "Hey, look at this face! Doesn't this look like Jin Guangyao?"

Others leaned in, clicking their tongues in mockery: "It really is him! What kind of sick narcissist carves his own face onto an idol?"

Sect Leader Yao chimed in, dripping with smug disdain, "Deifying himself. Pure, unadulterated arrogance."

"Arrogant doesn't even cover it! Unbelievable!"

Idiots, Wei Wuxian thought privately.

The world had dragged Jin Guangyao’s mother through the dirt, spitting on her as a filthy courtesan. So, he had carved her likeness into a statue of the divine, forcing thousands of devotees to fall to their knees and burn incense at her feet every single day.

Not that setting the record straight mattered anymore. Wei Wuxian knew better than anyone that nobody actually gave a damn, and nobody would ever believe it anyway. From this day forward, every scrap of Jin Guangyao’s legacy would be twisted into the ugliest, most malicious narrative the public could dream up, passed down from mouth to mouth like cheap gossip.

Before long, that wooden box would be sealed inside an even massive, indestructible outer sarcophagus, driven shut with seventy-two peachwood nails, buried deep in the earth, and trapped beneath a cursed mountain behind a massive warning stele.

The two souls trapped inside would be crushed beneath eternal wards and universal scorn, denied reincarnation for all eternity.

Leaning against the ruined doorway, Nie Huaisang watched the clan leaders haul the heavy coffin across the threshold. Looking down, he brushed the dried mud off the hem of his robes. His eyes caught on something in the dirt, pausing for a beat. Wei Wuxian’s gaze followed.

Lying in the filth was Jin Guangyao’s black gauze hat.

Nie Huaisang bent down, scooped it up, and dusted it off before sauntering out into the dawn.

Outside, Fairy was pacing anxiously, letting out a couple of whines. Hearing the sound, Jin Ling was suddenly dragged back to a memory from years ago: back when Fairy was just a clumsy, knee-high pup, Jin Guangyao had carried it into his quarters in his own arms.

Jin Ling had been tiny back then. He’d gotten into a brutal scrap with the other kids on Koi Tower, and even though he’d won, the humiliation had festered; he’d locked himself in his room, sobbing his eyes out while smashing every porcelain trinket he could get his hands on. The servants were terrified to go near him, ducking flying shards.

Then his Little Uncle had peeked his head inside, smiling warmly. A-Ling, what's got you so upset?

Jin Ling had answered by smashing half a dozen vases right at his boots.

Jin Guangyao had clucked his tongue, raising his hands in mock terror: Aiya, so fierce! You're scaring me to death! He’d shaken his head, feigning panic as he ducked back out.

The next morning, Jin Ling was still on a hunger strike, refusing to leave his bed. Jin Guangyao spent half the morning hovering outside the door. Just as Jin Ling had thrown his back against the wood, yelling at him to piss off, a tiny, muffled yip had drifted through the lattice.

He threw the door open.

Jin Guangyao was crouched in the corridor, cradling a round-eyed, glossy black puppy in his lap. Looking up, his smile was pure, unblemished warmth: I found this little guy, but I haven't got a clue what to name him. A-Ling, want to help me pick one out?

That smile had been so gentle, so devastatingly real. Jin Ling couldn't bring himself to believe it had all been a performance.

Without warning, tears welled up and spilled over his lashes again.

He’d always looked down on crying, sneering at it as the ultimate badge of weakness, but right now, hot tears were the only outlet left for the sheer, suffocating grief tearing through his ribs.

It was sickening: he couldn't bring himself to blame anyone, and he couldn't bring himself to truly hate anyone. Wei Wuxian, Jin Guangyao, Wen Ning—every single one of them bore some bloody share of the blame for his parents' deaths, and he had every textbook reason to despise them to his grave. Yet somehow, each one had reasons, tragedies, and circumstances that tied his hands, making it impossible to hold onto that pure rage.

If he couldn't hate them, who the hell was he supposed to hate? Was he just fated from birth to be an orphan? Was he denied vengeance, denied retribution, and now denied even the right to a clean, righteous hatred?

It was agonizing. It was profoundly unfair. Part of him wished they’d all just drop dead together so he could finally have some peace.

Noticing the boy weeping silently toward the coffin, Sect Leader Yao cleared his throat. "Young Master Jin, what are you crying for? Shedding tears for Jin Guangyao?"

Jin Ling bit his lip, refusing to answer.

Sect Leader Yao took that as an invitation to lean into his best lecturing-the-nephew tone: "Dry those tears, boy. A monster like your uncle doesn't deserve a single drop. If you ask me, you can't afford to be this soft! Weak-willed sentimental nonsense. You need to learn right from wrong, carry yourself properly, and—"

Back when the Lanling Jin Clan sat at the absolute peak of the cultivation world, these bottom-feeding sect leaders wouldn't have dared look Jin Ling in the eye, let alone play the stern elder to a Jin heir. But now that Jin Guangyao was dead, the clan’s backbone was broken, and their name was dragged through the mud with zero chance of recovery, the hyenas were finally brave enough to bite.

Jin Ling was already drowning in tangled misery, and hearing Yao preach at him made his temper detonate. He whirled around, screaming at the top of his lungs: "What if I want to cry?! Who the hell are you?! What do you think you are, telling me whether I can cry?!"

Sect Leader Yao hadn't expected to get barked at like a dog by a teenager, his face instantly souring into an ugly scowl.

Bystanders quickly chimed in with hushed placations: "Leave it, Sect Leader Yao. He's just a child."

Only then did Yao rein in his bruised ego, letting out a cold sneer. "Naturally. Hmph! Why lower myself to bicker with a wet-behind-the-ears brat who can't tell right from wrong?"

Over by the carts, Lan Qiren watched the coffin get strapped down securely. He turned around, blinking. "Where's Wangji?"

He had spent the last twenty minutes mentally drafting a grueling, four-month lecture series to force-feed his nephew the second they got back to the Cloud Recesses—or throw him back into solitary confinement if words failed. And now, the man was gone.

Pacing in a circle, he raised his voice: "Where is Wangji?!"

Lan Jingyi scratched his cheek. "Uh... earlier, I mentioned that we brought Little Apple along and tied him outside. So Hanguang-jun went... went to go check on the donkey..."

Lan Qiren’s eye twitched. "And then?!"

And then? Obviously, they bolted. Outside the Guanyin Temple, there wasn't a trace of Wei Wuxian, Lan Wangji, or Wen Ning left in the dirt.

Lan Qiren glanced back at Lan Xichen, who was trailing behind them like a ghost, eyes completely glazed over. Letting out a furious, soul-deep sigh, the old teacher whipped his sleeves back and stormed off.

Lan Jingyi blinked, looking around in confusion. "Wait... Sizhui? Where did Sizhui go?!"

Hearing that Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji had vanished, Jin Ling sprinted through the doors, nearly catching his boot on the high threshold. But as fast as he ran, the road ahead was completely empty. Fairy trotted around his heels, panting happily with its tongue out.

Beneath a towering, ancient tree in the temple courtyard, Jiang Cheng stood in the shadows. He looked over at the boy, his voice dead cold: "Wipe your face."

Jin Ling roughly dragged his forearm across his eyes, rubbing his cheeks red as he sprinted over. "Where are they?!"

"Gone," Jiang Cheng said.

Jin Ling gaped. "You just... let them leave?!"

Jiang Cheng’s lip curled into a bitter sneer. "What did you want me to do? Invite them over for dinner? Trade another round of 'thank yous' and 'I'm sorrys'?"

Frantic and furious, Jin Ling jabbed a finger at him. "No wonder he left! It's because you act like this! Jiujiu, why do you have to be so damn insufferable?!"

Jiang Cheng’s eyes flared, his hand flying up: "Is that how you talk to your elders?! Looking for a beating?!"

Jin Ling shrank back on instinct, and Fairy tucked its tail.

Yet the strike never landed. Jiang Cheng’s hand hovered in the damp morning air for a beat before slowly, limply falling back to his side.

"Shut up, Jin Ling," he rasped, looking utterly drained. "Just shut up. Let's go home. Everyone back to their own damn corners."

Jin Ling blinked, caught off guard by the lack of venom, and quietly held his tongue.

Hanging his head, he fell into step beside his uncle, their boots splashing through the puddles. After a few paces, he looked up again. "Jiujiu... earlier, did you have something you wanted to say to him?"

Jiang Cheng didn't look at him. "Say what? No."

"You did! I saw you! You were about to say something to Wei Wuxian, but then you swallowed it."

Silence stretched between them. Finally, Jiang Cheng gave a quiet, weary shake of his head.

"There's nothing to say."

What was there to say anyway?

Tell him that sixteen years ago, I didn't get captured by the Wen Clan because I was reckless, or because I was stupidly trying to sneak back to Lotus Pier to fetch my parents' corpses.

Tell him that when we were running for our lives, stopping in that tiny town to scrounge for food, a patrol of Wen cultivators had tracked our scent.

Tell him I noticed them early, slipped away from our hiding spot, and ducked into the shadows—safe and undiscovered—until I realized their sweep was heading straight for the street stall where you were buying flatbreads.

Tell him I sprinted out into the open on purpose, screaming to draw them away from you.

None of that mattered now.

Just like Wei Wuxian had been unable to tell him the truth about slicing out his golden core all those years ago, Jiang Cheng was never going to be able to tell him this.
